h1: The 5 Best Ergonomic Keyboards for Carpal Tunnel of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Carpal Tunnel Keyboards: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: five ergonomic keyboards that reduce wrist strain, from split layouts to wave frames, with specs, tradeoffs and who each fits.
summary: The Logitech Ergo K860 is our top pick for a curved split layout with negative tilt. The Wave Keys is the gentlest first step, the Perixx PERIBOARD-512B is the budget split, and the ProtoArc combo adds a matched ergonomic mouse. None of these treat carpal tunnel, so see a clinician for symptoms.
intro: The biggest mistake with an ergonomic keyboard is expecting it to fix a wrist problem. It can change your wrist position, which may reduce strain, but it is not medical treatment, and a padded wrist rest is for pauses between typing, not for resting on while you type.
We reviewed ergonomic keyboards on their listed layouts, tilt, connection and rests. Five made the list, ranked by how well they support a neutral wrist position and how easy they are to adapt to.

products.name: Logitech Ergo K860 Wireless Ergonomic Split Keyboard with Wrist Rest
products.verdict: The most complete curved split design, with negative tilt and either Bluetooth or a USB receiver.
products.description:
The K860 uses a curved split layout with negative tilt, an integrated wrist rest and a choice of Bluetooth or USB receiver. It costs $100-200.

The top rank goes to the way it combines layout and tilt in a single board. Compared with the Wave Keys below, it asks for a longer adjustment but changes wrist angle much more.

It suits people typing for long stretches who want to cut wrist strain proactively. Note that the wrist rest is meant for pauses between typing bursts, not for resting on during typing.
products.idealFor: Long daily typists who want a neutral wrist angle.

products.name: Logitech Wave Keys Wireless Ergonomic Keyboard - Graphite
products.verdict: A one-piece wave frame with almost no learning curve.
products.description:
The Wave Keys has a one-piece wave-shaped frame, a cushioned attached palm rest and Bluetooth or USB receiver connectivity. It is priced at $50-100.

It places second because it is easy to adopt but changes less than a true split. Next to the K860, it is cheaper and quicker to get used to.

It fits first-time ergonomic buyers who want a gentle start. The tradeoff is less aggressive positioning than a split design.
products.skipIf: You want a fully split layout.

products.name: Perixx PERIBOARD-512B Wired Ergonomic Keyboard - Split Keyboard with Wrist Rest
products.verdict: A low-cost wired split with a padded rest.
products.description:
The PERIBOARD-512B is a wired USB keyboard with a fixed-angle split layout and a padded wrist rest. It costs $25-50.

Third place reflects its lower price: it lacks wireless and tilt options. Against the Arteck wireless board it costs less and plugs in, with no battery to manage.

It works for buyers who want to try a split layout without much spend. Remember that the rest is for pauses, not for typing.
products.idealFor: Buyers testing a split layout cheaply.

products.name: Arteck Split Ergonomic Keyboard with Palm Rest, 2.4G USB Wireless
products.verdict: A wireless split board with a cushioned palm rest at a mid price.
products.description:
The Arteck keeps an angled, split key layout with a built-in cushioned palm rest and a 2.4G USB wireless receiver. It sits at $50-100.

It ranks fourth because it offers less documented tilt and design detail than the Logitech models. Compared with the Perixx, you pay more for wireless.

It suits desk workers who want to drop the cable. The listing gives limited detail beyond the layout and receiver.
products.idealFor: Wireless split seekers on a mid budget.

products.name: ProtoArc EKM01 Plus Wireless Ergonomic Keyboard Mouse Combo, Gray Black
products.verdict: A curved keyboard bundled with an ergonomic mouse.
products.description:
The ProtoArc EKM01 Plus is a wireless combo with a curved keyboard and an ergonomic mouse. It costs $50-100.

It ranks last because the keyboard is the less specialized part of the bundle. Against the Wave Keys, you get a matched mouse but less proven keyboard positioning.

It suits people who want one purchase to cover keyboard and mouse posture. The caveat is that the mouse may not suit everyone's grip.
products.idealFor: People replacing both keyboard and mouse.
products.skipIf: You already own an ergonomic mouse.

whatMatters.detail: A split keyboard separates the two halves so your hands sit shoulder width apart. This reduces how far your wrists bend inward. Look for the word split in the title and any angle detail.

Negative tilt slopes the keyboard away from you, which keeps wrists flatter than a standard raised back. It matters because raised back feet extend the wrist upward. Check the listing for negative tilt or tenting.
A wrist rest is meant to support your palms during pauses, not while typing. Resting on it during typing can add pressure. Pick a rest that is firm and low.
A new layout usually slows typing for days or weeks. One-piece wave frames are quicker to adapt than full splits. Decide how much slowdown you can accept.
Wired boards need no battery but add a cable. Wireless boards free your desk but need charging or batteries. Check whether the listing states Bluetooth, a USB receiver or both.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Neutral wrist angle, negative tilt, and a rest used only between bursts. See a clinician about symptoms.

cards.label: In this ranking
cards.text: The Logitech Ergo K860 pairs a curved split with negative tilt, and the Wave Keys offers a gentle start.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You type for hours each day, since the K860 adds tilt and split design.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You are just trying a split, where the Perixx PERIBOARD-512B keeps the cost low.

faq.a: No. An ergonomic keyboard may reduce strain through position, but it is not treatment. Talk to a healthcare professional about symptoms.

faq.q: Should I rest my wrists while typing?
faq.a: The listings advise using the rest between bursts, not during typing.

faq.q: Is a split keyboard worth it over a wave?
faq.a: If you want a bigger change in wrist angle, yes. A wave is easier to adopt.
Expect slower typing at first. Wave frames adapt quickest.

faq.q: Do I need a special mouse?
faq.a: Not required, but the ProtoArc includes one if you want matched posture.

faq.q: Can I use these with a Mac?
faq.a: Check the listing for OS compatibility, since support varies by model.

finalTake: The Logitech Ergo K860 is the best pick if you want a real change in wrist position. The Wave Keys is the safer first step, and the Perixx PERIBOARD-512B is the cheap way to try a split. None replaces medical advice.
